newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition criticises Bonn tax-cut scheme.
newsitem.headline: German opposition criticises Bonn tax-cut scheme.

text.p: Opposition parties and a tax-payer group on Thursday criticised a government proposal to rewrite Germany's heavy-handed tax code.

The reform package, which would lower taxes by a net 30 billion marks, is "a mixture of reform, retouches and tricks," Joachim Poss, finance spokesman of the Social Democrats (SPD) said on Deutschand Radio Berlin.

Poss also attacked the plan's proposed 15 percent rate on annual incomes above 13,000 marks, a level he said was too low to be taxed. "It violates the principal not to tax at the poverty level," he said in an interview.
He also denounced the plan's top rate of 39 percent on incomes above 90,000 marks, saying middle-income taxpayers would end up paying the same rate as millionaires.

Karlheinz Daeke, president of Germany's taxpayer association, BdS, said he was generally satisfied with the reform plan, but also criticised the 90,000 mark threshold for the 39 percent rate. At that level, many ordinary workers would get hit with the top rate, he said in a statement.
Meanwhile, Greens party finance chief Christine Scheel spoke out against Bonn's talks on increasing the valued-added tax to offset income tax cuts.
Details of the tax plan published on Thursday showed that overall tax cuts would total 81.9 billion marks, while slashing tax breaks would offset the cuts to the tune of 38.1 billion.
The net lightening of the tax load would be 43.8 billion marks -- although a rise in value-added tax to bring the overall cuts down to 30 billion marks has not yet been decided.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel was due to unveil the reform plan later.
